title: code-splitting
description: Learn about code-splitting. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Code splitting divides your application into smaller bundles that can be loaded on demand. This reduces the initial JavaScript payload, improves load times, and enables lazy loading of features that aren't immediately needed.
Why Code Splitting Matters

Modern web applications can easily become multi-megabyte in size. Loading everything upfront causes slow initial loads, especially on mobile devices. Code splitting allows users to download only what they need when they need it.

data.title: Before vs After Code Splitting
data.content: Impact of code splitting on bundle size.
data.code:
Before Code Splitting:
- Initial load: 2.5MB JavaScript
- Time to interactive: 8-12 seconds
- All features loaded (even unused ones)
- Poor mobile experience

After Code Splitting:
- Initial load: 250KB JavaScript (core)
- Time to interactive: 1-2 seconds
- Features loaded on demand
- Much better mobile experience

Example Split:
- Core bundle: 250KB (essential functionality)
- Dashboard bundle: 400KB (loaded when visiting dashboard)
- Admin bundle: 600KB (loaded only for admin users)
- Charts library: 300KB (loaded only when viewing charts)

data.text: Code Splitting Strategies
1. Entry Point Splitting
Multiple entry points create separate bundles for different parts of your application. This is ideal for multi-page applications or distinctly different user flows.

data.title: Multiple Entry Points
data.content: Configure separate bundles for different pages.

data.text: 2. Dynamic Imports
Dynamic imports enable code splitting at the module level. The import() function returns a promise that resolves to the module, allowing you to load code on demand.

data.title: Dynamic Import Syntax

data.text: 3. Route-Based Splitting
Split code by route so users only download the code for the page they're visiting. This is especially effective for applications with many pages or complex navigation.

data.title: React Router Code Splitting
data.content: Lazy load routes in React applications.

data.text: 4. Component-Based Splitting
Split heavy components so they load only when needed. This is useful for complex UI components like charts, rich text editors, or large tables.

data.title: React.lazy() for Components

data.text: 5. Vendor Splitting
Separate vendor dependencies from application code. This allows vendor code to be cached independently and reduces the impact of application changes on cache invalidation.

data.title: Webpack Vendor Splitting
data.content: Configure webpack to separate vendor code.

data.text: Prefetching and Preloading
Combine code splitting with prefetching and preloading to optimize the user experience. Prefetch likely-next code during idle time, preload critical code.

data.title: Webpack Magic Comments
data.content: Control loading behavior with magic comments.

data.text: Measuring Split Effectiveness
Use webpack-bundle-analyzer or similar tools to visualize your bundles and identify optimization opportunities. Track bundle sizes over time to catch regressions.

data.title: Bundle Analysis
Over-Splitting Risks
data.text: Don't split too aggressively. Too many small chunks increase HTTP overhead and can hurt performance. Aim for chunks between 20KB-200KB for optimal loading.
Best Practices

items: Split by route for maximum impact on initial load
Lazy load heavy components that aren't immediately visible
Separate vendor code for better caching
Monitor bundle sizes and catch regressions
UseSuspense boundaries for smooth loading states
Test on slow connections to validate improvements

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Code splitting reduces initial load time by loading code on demand
Multiple strategies: entry points, dynamic imports, route-based, component-based, vendor splitting
React.lazy() and Suspense enable easy component-level splitting
Route-based splitting provides the biggest performance impact
Vendor splitting improves caching and reduces cache invalidation
Use prefetching and preloading to optimize user experience
Avoid over-splitting to prevent HTTP overhead
Monitor bundle sizes to catch regressions
data.takeaway: Code splitting is essential for modern web performance, transforming large monolithic bundles into efficient, on-demand loaded chunks.
